## Presentations, Awards and Memorials:
### Parking and Traffic Commission Updates
Chairman Richard Benevento presented the annual report of the Parking and Traffic Commission. He provided an overview of the Commission's nine-seat membership, noting that it consists of representatives from the Police Department, Fire Department, Department of Public Services, Planning Department, Chamber of Commerce, City Council, and mayoral appointees. He explained that the Commission serves in an advisory capacity to the City Council, Mayor, Planning Board, and City departments on matters relating to parking, traffic, and transportation.

Chairman Benevento reviewed the Commission's responsibilities, including requests for parking restrictions, speed regulations, truck exclusions, traffic control devices, and construction management plans. He discussed several projects reviewed by the Commission over the past year, including development proposals and subdivisions, explaining that the Commission works with applicants to address traffic circulation, pedestrian safety, and neighborhood impacts before making recommendations to the appropriate board or department. Noting their work on the Trask Lane Development Project and reviewed ordinances and made recommendations to the Council for approval.

Chairman Benevento explained that the Commission's recommendations are based on engineering standards established by the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) which includes nine part, 83 chapters and 955 sections, as well as the Massachusetts amendments adopted by Massachusetts Department of Transportation. He noted that many requests received from residents cannot be implemented solely based on public opinion and often require engineering studies or must meet state standards before changes can be recommended. He noted that the commission works as an advisory board providing recommendation, with safety as their first consideration over convenience or other factors.

Houseman noted that the City's volunteers play an important role in making Beverly a special place and thanked Chairman Benevento and the members of the Parking and Traffic Commission for their time and service. He inquired about the status of a heavy vehicle exclusion study for Boyles Street. Chairman Benevento explained that truck exclusions generally require that heavy vehicles comprise a minimum of 5–8% of the daily traffic volume. He noted that a previous study found truck traffic accounted for only 1–2% of the total daily traffic. He stated that he was not aware of the Engineering Department currently conducting a new study but would follow up with the Department regarding the status of the request.

## Public Hearings:
**7:30 PM-Order #065**-National Grid Petition #31124344 to install underground facilities on Broadway. (Cont. from 2-17-2026 and 3-2-2026)
Vice President St. Hilaire opened the hearing at 7:30 PM. A representative of National Grid, 44 River Street, addressed the Council regarding the petition, noting it was submitted on behalf of the property owner, Beverly resident Mr. Greg, to provide electrical service to the property at 32 Broadway. He explained that the project proposes the installation of underground conduit from an existing manhole in front of 28 Broadway to a new handhole at 30 Broadway, with the conduit extending to 32 Broadway. He stated that the proposed 600-amp electrical service required by the development could only be provided through the proposed underground installation.

Tiffany Collins, 35 Broadway, spoke in opposition to the petition, expressing concern over additional excavation of Broadway following several recent utility and infrastructure projects. She noted that the roadway had only recently been reconstructed and questioned the need to disturb the newly paved street. While acknowledging the need to provide electrical service to the development, she urged National Grid to explore alternatives that would minimize further impacts to the roadway and surrounding neighborhood.

Spang asked whether the work could be limited to beneath the sidewalk to avoid disturbing the roadway. The National Grid representative stated that an alternative option had been considered, but explained that alternatives carried a significant fee and that National Grid looks to work in the most cost-effective and safest manner possible. The representative further noted that the customer would be responsible for restoring the roadway and committed to restoring the affected section curb-to-curb.

Houseman agreed with the concerns expressed by the residents, noting that they were shared by many Broadway residents regarding the continued impact of roadway construction. He questioned why this work had not been coordinated with the recent cable transmission project. Houseman confirmed that the customer had committed to curb-to-curb roadway restoration and stated that the sidewalks would not be damaged.

Sonia, noting that he resides at 31 Broadway, echoed the concerns raised by his neighbor, Ms. Collins. He stated that he would support referring the petition back to the subcommittee to include amended language to ensure the petitioner receives the electrical service needed while also ensuring that the roadway and sidewalks on Broadway are restored to their current condition. He further emphasized that the curb-to-curb paving commitment should be completed in a timely manner.

Spang asked whether National Grid would be performing the work. The representative explained that all the civil work would be completed by the customer. Spang noted the Engineering Department's requirements for contractors performing work within the public way. The representative noted he was committed to maintaining open communication with the city throughout the project.

Vice President St. Hilaire closed the public hearing at 7:45 PM and referred the order to the Committee on Public Services.

**Order #088**-An FY2026 Inter Departmental Transfer request of $241,250 from the Reserve for union negotiations to fund retroactive costs back to July 1, 2024.
Houseman questioned the general principle of precedent and how this type of arrangement for post-employment benefit payments might affect future negotiations with other bargaining units. He acknowledged that the matter was separate from the collective bargaining process but raised it as a broader policy question.

Cahill explained that the transfer was related to the Department of Public Services (DPS) classification and compensation study, which began more than two years prior. He stated that the study involved comparing DPS positions with comparable communities, revising job descriptions where necessary, and ensuring employees were compensated competitively and fairly. Due to delays in completing the study, including unforeseen circumstances affecting the consultant, the administration committed to making any approved salary adjustments retroactive to the beginning of the current contract. The Mayor stated that this commitment also applied to employees who had retired after the contract began but were employed during the study period, noting that honoring the commitment was a matter of fairness.

Houseman asked whether providing retroactive compensation to former employees could establish a precedent affecting future negotiations with other bargaining units. Assistant City Solicitor Christopher Dole explained that a similar process had previously been completed for the Beverly Municipal Employees Association (BMEA) and emphasized that the City's other bargaining units do not have the same diversity of job classifications requiring such a review. He explained that the compensation adjustments were separate from collective bargaining and resulted from a unique classification and compensation study. Mr. Dole stated that he did not believe the action would establish a precedent for future collective bargaining negotiations.

Houseman also asked whether the financial impact of the salary adjustments had been incorporated into the City's long-range financial forecast. Mayor Cahill confirmed that the costs had been included.

Budget Analyst Gerry Perry addressed the Council, stating that he had initially expressed concerns regarding the proposal, particularly its potential precedent and financial impact. Following discussions with the administration and review of the matter, he concluded that the adjustments were justified. Mr. Perry noted that the total compensation package amounted to approximately $502,000 for 43 current employees and four retirees and confirmed that the projected costs had been incorporated into the City's FY2027 financial forecast. He further stated that the consultant's report found DPS compensation to be below comparable communities and that the adjustments would help improve recruitment, retention, and equity with other City bargaining units.

Vice President St. Hilaire put the question of acceptance of the proposal and adoption of the order. A motion was made and seconded. A vote was taken, and the motion carried (7-1 with St. Hilaire in opposition).

Spang noted the upcoming public forum hosted by Special Committee on Rental policies public forum Wednesday, April 8, 2026, at 6:00 PM in Council Chambers.

Spang further noted that the Legal Affairs and Public Services Committees would be meeting prior to the next regular Council meeting on April 21, 2026, at 6:00 PM, in Council Chamber to meet with the Police Department to discuss the automated license plate readers.

A motion to adjourn was made and seconded. A vote was taken, and motion carried (8-0). The meeting adjourned at 8:34 PM.
